summary: Haarith bin Umayrah recounts visiting Salmaan Faarsi, who was scraping hide in his tannery, and Salmaan says that souls who came together for Allaah's pleasure become friends.

Abu Qilaabah reports that Salmaan Faarsi, while making dough himself, received a man who had come to pass on greetings from someone else, and told him that the greeting was a trust that would have been left unfulfilled.
notes: The unnamed messenger and sender are left out. honest-dealings is a stretch: the closing remark is about delivering a message as a trust.

summary: Amr bin Abu Qurra Kindi reports that his father offered his sister in marriage to Salmaan Faarsi, who refused and married a freed slave woman; when Abu Qurra went to Salmaan after an argument with Hudhayfah, Salmaan received him in very simple surroundings.
notes: Hudhayfah is taken as Hudhayfah bin Yamaan (the usual companion in this story). hudhayfa-bin-mihsin is the other vocab entry, so check. Abu Qurra's sister is unnamed.

summary: Three reports on Salmaan Faarsi's humility as a commander and governor: soldiers mocked him as he rode a donkey, the people of Madaa'in called him Gurg Aamad, and a witness saw him in short, shabby clothes; he said good and bad will be seen only in the Aakhirah.
notes: Three separate reports joined: Maymoon bin Mahraan, an unnamed Abdul Qais man, and Huraym. The unnamed soldiers, youths and Abdul Qais men are left out.

summary: Thaabit reports that while Salmaan Faarsi was governor of Madaa'in he carried a stranger's load of figs to the man's house, saying he had intended to do it to please Allaah and could not put it down before he arrived.
notes: The narrator Thaabit is ambiguous: vocab id thaabit (unsure) is used; thaabit-bunaani is another possibility. The man from Shaam is left out.

summary: Abdullaah bin Buraydah reports that Salmaan Faarsi made things with his hands, sold them, and used the money to buy meat or fish to share with lepers.

Muhammad bin Seereen reports that whenever Umar bin Khattaab appointed a governor he would write that the governor should greet first, be content with a lower seat, and dislike ostentation and boasting.
notes: The heading names Hudhayfah bin Yamaan but the text is about Umar's letters to governors; check the heading. Stray ')' and 'are:)' are OCR debris.

summary: Abu Hurayrah reports that the Sahabah asked the Prophet whether he joked with them, and he said he joked but spoke only the truth.
notes: The Sahabah who asked are a group and are left out.

summary: Abdullaah bin Abbaas describes a joke of the Prophet with one of his wives, whom he told to wear a large shawl and drag it along like a bride's.
notes: Ends with the footnote marker '(3)'. The wife and the questioner are unnamed.

summary: Anas describes the Prophet's gentleness with Abu Umayr, a young brother of his, asking after the child's pet bird, and then recounts the Prophet leading prayer on a mat at their home.
notes: Two anecdotes in one item (the bird joke and the prayer at home). OCR drops the bird's name at 'How is This was the little red-beaked bird'.

summary: Anas reports that the Prophet would ask his young brother Abu Umayr how his little bird, Nughayr, was doing.
Anas reports that at the home of Abu Talha, the Prophet noticed Abu Umayr looking sad, learned that his bird had died, and affectionately asked how Nughayr was.
notes: OCR joins 'Abu Umayrwas'.

summary: Anas reports that a man asked the Prophet for transport, and the Prophet offered him a camel's young to ride, then asked whether every camel is not the child of another.
notes: Only one approved theme fits this narration, so no second theme was found. The man is unnamed.

summary: Anas reports that the Prophet affectionately teased him by calling him 'O two-eared one'.
notes: Anas is both narrator and the person addressed, so his role is subject.

summary: Anas reports that the Prophet loved Zaahir, a countryman who brought him gifts, joked with him in the market, and told him that he was precious in Allaah's sight.
notes: Zaahir is not in the vocab; the text gives him (RA).

summary: Nu'maan bin Basheer reports that Abu Bakr, finding his daughter Aa'isha raising her voice before the Prophet, moved to slap her and was stopped by the Prophet; when Abu Bakr later found them reconciled he joked that they should let him into their peace as they had let him into their war, and the Prophet agreed.

Aa'isha recounts how she beat the Prophet in a race when she was slim, and he beat her in a later race when she had gained weight, saying 'This is for that'; Anas and Abu Qilaabah report him telling the camel-driver Anjasha to go easy with the women.
notes: Three reports joined. Anjasha's sahabi status is uncertain. The Prophet's wives are unnamed.

summary: Hasan reports that an old woman asked the Prophet to pray that she enter Jannah; he told her old women will not enter it, and then sent word, citing the verse that Allaah created the women of Jannah especially.
notes: 'Hasan' is not in the vocab and is probably Hasan al-Basri, which the text does not say; name kept as written. The old woman is unnamed.

summary: Umm Salamah reports that Abu Bakr sent Nu'aymaan and Suwaybit bin Harmala on a trade journey, where Nu'aymaan tricked Suwaybit into being taken as a slave; Abu Bakr returned the ten camels paid for him and freed him, and the Prophet laughed about it for a year.
notes: Nu'aymaan is tagged as vocab id nuaym-bin-abdillaah, matching the heading's trickster; please check, since n01900 names a different Nu'aymaan. The buyers are unnamed.

summary: Rabee'ah bin Uthmaan reports that Nu'aymaan bin Amr Ansaari, urged by some Sahabah, slaughtered a Bedouin's camel to eat it; when the Prophet found Nu'aymaan hiding in a house, Nu'aymaan blamed the Sahabah, and the Prophet compensated the Bedouin.

people.name: Subaagha bint Zubayr bin Abdul Muttalib

notes: Ends with '(U' OCR debris. This Nu'aymaan may be the same man as the Nu'aymaan bin Amr bin Rifaa'ah in n01901; kept separate. The Bedouin and the Sahabah are unnamed.

summary: Abdullaah bin Mus'ab reports that Makhramah bin Naufal, an old blind man, was led by Nu'aymaan to urinate in a corner of the Masjid; afterwards, on Nu'aymaan's word, Makhramah struck Uthmaan, who was praying, and Uthmaan forgave Nu'aymaan because he was a Badr veteran.

people.name: Nu'aymaan bin Amr bin Rifaa'ah bin Haarith bin Sawaad

notes: Ends with the heading fragment 'Generosity' (section debris). This Nu'aymaan may be the same as the Ansaari Nu'aymaan in n01900. The Banu Zuhra are a tribe, not a person, and are left out.

summary: Abdullaah bin Abbaas says the Prophet was the most generous of people, most of all in Ramadhaan when he met Jibra'eel every night, and more generous than the blowing wind.
notes: OCR drops a word ('revised the with him'), so the object of the revision is unclear. Jibra'eel is an angel and is left out.

summary: Jaabir and Abu Sa'eed Khudri each report that the Prophet never refused anything that was asked of him.
notes: Two reports in one item. Abdullaah bin Abu Bakr is the named source in the lengthy hadith; vocab has two entries for this name (abdullaah-bin-abi-bakr and abdullaah-bin-abu-bakr), and the first was used.

summary: Ali reports that when asked for something, the Prophet said yes when he intended to do it and stayed silent when he did not, but never said no.
notes: Ends with ',,' OCR debris.

summary: Rubayyi bint Mu'awwidh reports that her father sent a Saa of fresh dates with cucumber to the Prophet, who in return filled her hand with jewels that had just come from Bahrain.
notes: Another narration says gold, not jewels. Mu'awwidh bin Afraa is the spelling in the text, so muawwadh-bin-afraa is used, not muaadh-bin-afraa. The closing 'Hadhrat Hasan bin (RA)' line is an editorial cross-reference, not narration.

summary: Abdullaah bin Umar reports that a woman brought a garment for the most generous of the Arabs, and the Prophet directed it to Sa'eed bin Al Aas, after which such garments were called Sa'eediyyah.
notes: The vocab marks saeed-bin-al-aas as sahabi 'no', but the text gives him (RA). Please check. The woman is unnamed. The closing sentence is an editorial cross-reference.

summary: Abdullaah bin Umar says there was a time when the Muslims thought of each other above themselves, but now people love dinars and dirhams more than their brothers.
notes: The text says the narration continues. The cross-references to other chapters are editorial.

summary: Abu Sa'eed Khudri reports visiting the Prophet during a high fever and being told that the prophets suffer most, then the scholars, then the pious; Abu Ubaydah bin Hudhayfah reports, from his aunt Faatimah, that the Prophet lay under a dripping water bag in his fever and said the closest to the prophets suffer most.
notes: Two reports in one item. The aunt Faatimah is not matched to a vocab id (faatima and faatima-bint-utba are both possible). Abu Ubaydah bin Hudhayfah is not Abu Ubaydah bin Jarraah.

summary: Aa'isha reports that the Prophet, in great pain, turned from side to side on his bed, and told her that every thorn or pain a believer suffers forgives a sin and raises his rank.
notes: Ends with a stray heading fragment ('The Sahabah ... Exercise Patience with Illness'), which is section debris.

summary: Jaabir reports that fever asked permission to visit the Prophet and was sent to the people of Quba; when they complained, he offered to pray it away or let it stay as a purification from sin, and they chose to keep it.
notes: Fever is personified and is not a person, so left out. 'Ummu Mildam' is OCR for the name given to fever. The people of Quba are a group.

summary: Salmaan reports that the Prophet sent fever to the people of Quba, who chose to keep it as a means of forgiveness; Abu Hurayrah reports that fever went to the Ansaar, the Prophet prayed and they were cured, and a woman of the Ansaar chose patience and Jannah over a cure.
notes: Three accounts joined: Salmaan (Quba), Abu Hurayrah (Ansaar), and the woman's reply. The woman is unnamed and left out.

summary: Aa'isha reports that when a regular attendee at the Prophet's gatherings was struck down by a high fever, the Prophet visited him and told him that fever is his Ummah's share of Jahannam in this world.
notes: The sick man is unnamed. OCR garbles the Prophet's title at one point ('Rasulullaah H').

summary: Abu Safar reports that when people visited Abu Bakr during his illness and asked whether they should summon a physician, Abu Bakr said the physician had already seen him and that Allaah does as He pleases.
notes: The visitors and the physician are unnamed.

summary: Mu'aawiya bin Qurra reports that when friends visited Abu Dardaa in illness, he said his sickness was for his sins and that he wished for Jannah, and when they offered to summon a physician he said that it was Allaah who had laid him there.
notes: The text cuts off mid-sentence ('with this'). The friends are unnamed.

summary: Abdur Rahmaan bin Ghanam reports that when the plague struck Shaam, Amr bin Al Aas told people to flee it and Shurahbeel bin Hasanah rejected that; Mu'aadh bin Jabal prayed for his family's full share of the plague, lost two daughters and then his son Abdur Rahmaan, was himself struck, and advised a weeping man to seek knowledge from four men.
notes: Several reports joined, including the 'another narration' line. Mu'aadh's daughters and the weeping man are unnamed. Abu Abdur-Rahmaan is Mu'aadh's kunya. Ibraheem is included as a prophet named as an example. Abdur Rahmaan bin Mu'aadh is not in the vocab.

summary: Shahr bin Howshab, reporting from Raaba, says that when the plague spread Abu Ubaydah prayed for his family's share and then died of it; Mu'aadh bin Jabal, after taking command, also lost his son and was struck himself; Amr bin Al Aas then told people to flee to the mountains, Abu Waathilah rebuked him, and Umar, hearing the matter, said Amr had not condemned it.
notes: A footnote ('(l) lbn Khuzaymah ... Kanzul Ummaal', 'Majma'uz Zawaa'id') sits inside the text and was ignored. Shahr bin Howshab is not in the vocab (the vocab has howshab-dhi-dhulaym and howshab-himyari). Abu Waathilah is not in the vocab.

summary: Abu Qilaabah reports Mu'aadh bin Jabal's reply to Amr bin Al Aas, that the plague is martyrdom, a mercy and the Prophet's du'aa, and explains the du'aa: the Prophet asked that his Ummah not perish by drought, be overrun by an enemy, or split into factions; the last was refused, so he said 'let it be fever or a plague'.
notes: The family member who overheard the Prophet is unnamed.

summary: Urwa bin Zubayr reports that Abu Ubaydah and his family were spared the plague until a sore appeared on his little finger, and that he hoped Allaah would bless it, since Allaah makes a little thing much.
notes: 'Uxwa' is OCR for 'Urwa'. The vocab id urwa-bin-zubayr is marked unsure.

summary: Haarith bin Abu Umayrah Haarithi reports that Mu'aadh bin Jabal sent him to ask Abu Ubaydah how he was in the plague; Abu Ubaydah showed him a plague sore on his palm and swore he would not trade it even for red camels.
notes: This Haarith may be a different person from Haarith bin Umayrah in n01881.

summary: Zaid bin Arqam says that when he developed a cataract the Prophet visited him and told him that if he lost his eye and bore it patiently for Allaah's reward, his reward would be Jannah.
